Could be a locolith or a lacolith. These are intrusive bodies that don’t reach the surface and remain at substantial depth.  The magma cools slowly from the top down.  The melt is homogeneous but differentiates as it cools.  The Mariinsky Reef in South Africa is an example of such formations.  😊😊

Sadly most of this video does relate to Layercake Mountain’s formation.😢😢

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: That's an interesting comparison! The researchers who studied Layer Cake Mountain found that the bands formed as the volcanic rock cooled and remaining melt filled cracks inside it. A bit different from the Merensky Reef, but I can see why you'd make that connection. I also wanted to cover some of the history around the mountain, though I appreciate the feedback on keeping the geology front and centre!

comments.text: Native legends tell of mountains rising and melting away in the space of a single day. Some Salish legends tell of Scnoki,  a 2 headed sea serpent that would travel from the sea shore, go across the land and up the hills leaving a ragged scar as it went and end up at a lake where there had been none before. In my interpretation this was an electric discharge.  I live along the Sooke river valley, known for its Potholes which is a prime example of what the legends describe.

replies.author: @thedarkmoon2341
replies.text:
@HiddenCanada The legend of Scnoki was not mentioned in regard to the Sooke potholes but after looking at the legends of the Deep Cove and Indian Arm and puzzling over some geological features along the Sooke river the electric discharge model explained much to me. The accidental discovery of some very localised and strong remnant magnetic dips along the basalt banks of the river confirmed for me the presence of intense electrical activity. 
There are a few web pages on the net where I look at what I refer to as Electro-Magnetic Geomorphology. Of course academic geologists think I am crazy!

The volcanic rock here is millions of years older than the glaciers that later moved through the valley. And despite how perfectly spaced those bands look, they're natural, not man-made terraces. replies.author: @HiddenCanada

Glaciers came much later and helped carve out the valley we recognize today. So it's really a combination of tectonic activity and glacial erosion.

comments.author: @paxdriver
comments.text:
From the area but not a geologist, but I'd heard from some residents that the early mountain formation meant there could've been a giant ice sheet capping a lot of really weak, slow moving, thick lava flows. The cap keeps the rock heated across many layers, while also cooling it from the glacier. The melt of the ice on top would keep the layers from cooling independently and also dripping water in cracks before the rock fully cooled.

After the cap was gone the winter could create single cooling unit events for a few years as the volcano stopped releasing pressure.

The the soft top layers of rock get lifted by the remaining pressure beneath the surface, pushing up on the newly exposed layers before the soft hot top now exposed to elements was deformed from holding pressure down, lifting it for several more years.

I'm probably not explaining it exactly as they described going off memory, but it had something to do with a slow sludgy magma flow, an ice cap holding in heat before disappearing, and then hardening top layer holding in remaining pressure pushing the mountain upward with its layers being exposed by cooling top down after baking under ice.

replies.author: @albinorhino6
replies.text:
Local here who lives in Black Mtn.

As far as I know, the whole of Scenic Canyon is part of a regional park, so is protected in that regard.  The private property is on the north face, ie the opposite side, of the mountain.  The First Nations territory is in the canyon floor, and the banks and slopes on the south side of Mission Creek.

I don’t see any development happening immediately near Layer Cake.  The terrain is just too severe.  The private properties on the back side are a concern.  If it’s ever developed though, it would be done so outside the boundaries of the regional park.  The First Nations territory likely won’t see anything happen in the near future.  The terrain is surprisingly steep and difficult to access.  That said, they can do what they want with the territory.  They could build a tire burning factory there if they wanted to, and I’m not sure much could stop them.

It’s a tricky situation.  The area will never get full conservation status, as it’s quite literally within the city limits of a rapidly growing city.  That said, Kelowna has a huge amount of green space and park space within the city, it’s one of the main attractions.  So I wouldn’t be surprised to see Scenic Canyon including Layer Cake Mtn remain as a park for the foreseeable future.
